text: JAPZ ERP: JAPZ Grill Burger & BistroInventory Management ModuleSystem Architecture Diagram/Figure 1. System Architecture of the JAPZ Inventory ModuleFigure 1 presents the overall system architecture of the JAPZ ERP Inventory Management Module, showing how its users, web application, access controls, backend services, and database work together. Inventory Staff use the web interface for daily tasks such as viewing stock balances, receiving deliveries, recording physical counts, documenting waste, and managing recipes. Administrators handle controlled tasks, including approvals and corrections. The interface organizes these capabilities into overview and stock screens, transaction screens, and recipe, report, and settings screens. Before a request is processed, the access-control layer checks whether the account is approved and whether its role permits the requested action.

Authorized requests are sent as JSON to the Express Inventory API. Its stock and recipe services handle receiving, counts, waste, supplier returns, recipe information, and batch availability; other handlers manage movement history, CSV reporting, alerts, and refresh settings. The server uses Sequelize to read and update MySQL records for items, suppliers, batches, receipts, counts, movements, recipes, and configuration. The diagram emphasizes the separation of responsibilities: the browser presents information, access checks restrict operations, backend services apply inventory rules, and the database retains the resulting records. This organization supports consistent data handling across the module's different screens.

Class Diagram/Figure 2. Core Inventory Classes and RelationshipsFigure 2 illustrates the principal inventory classes and the associations that connect suppliers, stored items, deliveries, batches, and quantity changes. Supplier stores identifying information and an active flag, while StockItem describes a tracked supply through its name, kind, measurement unit, on-hand quantity, and reserved quantity. The associations indicate that suppliers may be related to multiple items and receipts, and that an item may be represented by several batches. StockBatch records the quantity and reservation status of a particular batch, along with its expiry date and quarantine status. Separating batches from stock items is important because different deliveries of the same ingredient may have different expiry or availability conditions.

StockReceipt represents a delivery transaction, identified by its receipt number and date, and contains one or more StockReceiptLine entries. Each line connects the receipt with a specific stock item and batch while recording the received quantity, conversion factor, and unit cost. StockMovement captures the changes associated with inventory actions, including the action type, reason, and adjustments to on-hand or reserved quantities; a movement may be associated with a batch where applicable. The note below identifies additional records for stock counts, waste reports, menu recipes, allocations, settings, and inventory operations, with prepared quantities kept in the shared MenuItem model. Taken together, the classes model both current balances and the transactions needed to explain how those balances changed.

Component Diagram/Figure 3. Components of the Inventory ModuleFigure 3 divides the JAPZ Inventory Management Module into interacting software components rather than treating it as one program. The Inventory UI contains the screens used for stock and receiving, physical counts and waste, recipe-related activities, reports, and settings. The Access component provides JWT authentication and approved-user or role checks. These checks establish whether an incoming request is associated with a valid user and whether that user is permitted to perform the requested operation. The connections show that user-facing functions depend on the inventory API and authorization mechanisms rather than accessing stored inventory records directly.

The backend is divided into Stock Services and Handlers. Stock Services contain the operational rules for receiving stock, counting, recording waste and returns, managing recipes and menu availability, and controlling versioned stock operations. Handlers support reports, movement history, inventory settings, refresh policies, and access to Sequelize models. Both groups interact with the MySQL inventory records shown outside the module boundary. The component organization separates user interaction, identity and permission checks, stock-changing logic, and reporting or persistence concerns. This distinction helps explain which part of the application is responsible when stock is updated, historical information is requested, or access to an operation is restricted.

Deployment Diagram/Figure 4. Local Deployment of the Inventory ModuleFigure 4 describes the module's local deployment arrangement and identifies where the frontend, backend, and database run. Inventory Staff or Admin users open the React interface in a browser on a staff computer. Browser requests travel over a local HTTP connection using JSON messages to the deployment host. On that host, Vite serves frontend assets on port 5173, while the Node.js environment runs the Express Inventory API on port 3000. This separates the interface served to the browser from the server-side processing responsible for inventory operations.The Express API uses Sequelize and SQL to communicate with the MySQL environment, which is labeled with the japz_pos database and port 3306. MySQL stores the records accessed and changed by inventory workflows, while the API mediates database operations instead of exposing direct database access to the browser. The named ports and local connection describe the configured development or local-testing setup shown in the figure; they should not be interpreted as a confirmed production deployment.

Object Diagram/Figure 5. Example Objects After Receiving FlourFigure 5 shows a concrete instance of the inventory classes after a sample flour delivery, making the relationships from Figure 2 easier to understand. The supplier object identifies a sample supplier with ID 1. The stock item object represents Flour, identified by item ID 10, and uses grams as its base unit. A stock receipt with ID 20 and reference REC-020 is associated with that supplier. Its receipt line records a purchased quantity of five kilograms and a conversion factor of 1,000 grams per kilogram. The converted inventory quantity is therefore 5,000 grams.The receipt line connects the delivery to batch ID 30, whose on-hand quantity is shown as 5,000 grams and reserved quantity as zero. A StockMovement object records the receive action and a positive on-hand adjustment of 5,000 grams. These linked instances demonstrate that a received delivery is represented not only by a final balance but also by a supplier, receipt, delivery line, batch, and movement record. The IDs and quantities are illustrative examples used to explain the model, not verified business transactions.

Package Diagram/Figure 6. Packages of the Inventory ModuleFigure 6 organizes the inventory source code into packages according to responsibility and shows the dependencies between them. The presentation package contains screens for receiving, supplies, counts, recipes, reports, and settings. Those screens use the client package, which supplies the inventory data context, API client, and request identifiers. Requests then cross the HTTP API boundary into the routes package, where inventory endpoints are defined and access middleware is applied. This creates a separation between what users see, how client requests are formed, and how requests enter the backend.The routes package uses services that implement stock operations, order allocations, availability checks, and settings-related behavior. Services access the models package for items, batches, receipts, counts, movements, and recipes, as well as shared resources such as MenuItem, User, Order, and the database connection. Both model and shared resources ultimately depend on MySQL inventory storage. The dependency arrows help explain which packages rely on others without suggesting that each package is deployed as a separate server. Organizing the code this way keeps interface behavior, request handling, business rules, and persistence concerns distinguishable as the module grows.

Composite Structure Diagram/Figure 7. Internal Collaboration Within the Inventory APIFigure 7 provides a closer view of the internal structure of the Inventory API. The enclosing boundary represents the API itself, while the small ports show the points where it receives HTTP requests and accesses SQL persistence. An incoming request first reaches the access part, which checks authentication and role permissions. Once authorized, the request passes to an inventory route handler responsible for directing it to the relevant operation. This makes authorization an explicit stage before stock-related processing.The route handler collaborates with the stock inventory service, which performs the inventory-specific work, and the service in turn uses data models to read or change stored records. The connection from the data part to the SQL persistence port represents the boundary between application logic and database access. Unlike the deployment diagram, this figure focuses on collaboration within one API boundary rather than physical machines or processes. It shows how requests are coordinated across internal parts while keeping security, routing, business rules, and persistence responsibilities separate.

Profile Diagram/Figure 8. Inventory Documentation ProfileFigure 8 defines JAPZInventoryProfile, a UML documentation profile intended to label inventory-specific elements consistently. Its InventoryRecord stereotype extends a UML Class and introduces properties for the base unit and whether audit fields are used. The StockService stereotype extends a Component and records its responsibility and inventory module association. StockOperation extends an Operation and describes the corresponding stock action, including whether that operation changes a balance. These stereotypes allow class, component, and operation diagrams to convey inventory meaning through a shared notation.The profile also defines BaseUnit values for grams, milliliters, and pieces, and StockAction values for receiving, counting, reserving, consuming, releasing, wasting, and supplier returns. The constraints note three important design expectations: quantities should not become negative, reserved stock should be protected, and movement history should be retained. These labels and constraints document the intended interpretation of inventory elements. They are modeling conventions rather than proof that an additional profile engine, user interface, or runtime feature exists in the deployed application.

Data Flow Diagram (DFD)/Figure 9. Inventory Data FlowFigure 9 traces the flow of information between Inventory Staff, three inventory processes, and three data stores. Staff first provide item or supplier details to Process 1.0, Maintain Supplies and Suppliers. That process writes the corresponding records to D1, Items/Suppliers, creating the reference information needed for later stock activity. When staff enter receiving or adjustment information, Process 2.0, Receive or Adjust Stock, works with the relevant stored inventory records. Receipt and batch data are kept in D2, Receipts/Batches, while entries describing quantity changes are recorded in D3, Stock Movements. The connections also indicate that updated stock balances are reflected in the inventory information available to the module.Process 3.0, View Stock and Reports, consumes information from these stores: item balances from D1, batch details from D2, and movement history from D3. It turns that data into stock displays and reports returned to Inventory Staff. The diagram therefore distinguishes data entry and maintenance from reporting, while showing that both depend on shared stored records. It is a data-flow view of what information is created, updated, and retrieved, not a step-by-step sequence of API messages or a depiction of database table relationships.

Use Case Diagram/Figure 10. Inventory Staff Use CasesFigure 10 identifies the main goals available to Inventory Staff within the JAPZ Inventory Management system boundary. The actor is connected to viewing the inventory overview, maintaining supplies and suppliers, receiving stock, recording physical counts, recording waste or returns, managing recipes and batches, viewing history or reports, and configuring inventory settings. These use cases describe the staff-facing scope of the module rather than prescribing the sequence in which the screens must be opened. Each use case represents a function a permitted user may request through the system.The diagram also shows relationships that refine several activities. Receive Stock includes Validate Delivery and Convert Units, meaning those steps are integral to processing a delivery. Submit for Admin Review extends Record Physical Count when the configured approval policy requires review rather than immediate application. Export CSV similarly extends viewing history and reports when a user selects an export. These conditional extensions are not mandatory parts of every count or report view. Although an Admin actor is not drawn in this figure, the review extension points to a later administrator-controlled decision. The use cases clarify the module's functional scope and distinguish core actions from checks or optional follow-up actions.

Activity Diagram/Figure 11. Main Activity Flow of the Inventory ModuleFigure 11 presents the main activity paths followed by a user in the inventory workspace. The process begins when the workspace opens and the system authenticates the account and checks the user's role. The authorization decision then determines whether processing can continue: an unauthorized user sees an access-denied result and leaves the activity, while an authorized user proceeds to select a function. The next decision separates two kinds of work—operations that may change stock and tasks that read inventory information without making a stock adjustment.On the stock-operation path, the user selects receiving, counting, waste, or return work. The system checks quantities and permissions before saving related changes together; if the action is a physical count that requires approval, it is instead queued for review. On the view/report path, the user opens balances, history, or reports, selects any relevant filters, and reads the resulting data. An export to CSV may also be requested. Both branches eventually converge on refreshing or leaving the workspace. This workflow highlights the different safeguards applied to stock changes and read-only reporting, as well as the early termination of unauthorized access.

Sequence Diagram/Figure 12. Sequence of a Successful Stock ReceiptFigure 12 details the ordered messages exchanged when Inventory Staff submit a stock receipt. The interaction begins when a staff member enters delivery data in the Receiving UI. The UI sends the delivery information and a request identifier to the API/Service. Before creating any new records, the backend searches the models and MySQL storage for a prior result associated with that request. When no previous result exists, the process continues into a loop that handles each delivery line. Within that loop, the service validates the line and converts its quantity to the relevant inventory unit before sending the receipt and stock writes to persistence.After all required changes have been written, the database commits the transaction and the API returns the saved receipt to the interface. The UI then refreshes the displayed stock information so the user can see the result. The alternative paths at the bottom explain how the flow handles two important exceptions. If the request was already saved, the system returns the original receipt instead of adding stock a second time. If validation fails or the save does not complete successfully, the transaction is rolled back and an error is returned. The sequence emphasizes that receiving is more than inserting a receipt: it coordinates validation, unit conversion, related stock updates, duplicate-request handling, and transaction completion.

State Machine Diagram/Figure 13. Stock Count Status ChangesFigure 13 describes the life cycle of a physical stock count and the decisions that determine its final status. After a count is submitted, the first decision asks whether approval is required. A count that does not require review can move directly to applied, meaning the accepted count updates the stock balance. If approval is necessary, the count enters pending. The entry action for pending explicitly keeps the existing balance unchanged while the record waits for an administrator's decision, preventing an unapproved discrepancy from being applied prematurely.A pending count can follow three outcomes. An administrator may reject it, sending the count to rejected without modifying stock. If review finds that the count is no longer valid—for example, because the stock version or reservation conditions have changed—it becomes stale and requires a new count rather than being approved against outdated information. When review is valid and approval is granted, the count moves to applied and the stock is updated. These states distinguish a proposed correction from an accepted one and show why approval alone is not sufficient unless the underlying inventory conditions are still valid.

Communication Diagram/Figure 14. Object Communication During ReceivingFigure 14 shows how five collaborating objects communicate while stock is received, using numbered messages to indicate the order and nesting of the interactions. InventoryStaff initiates message 1 by submitting delivery information to the ReceivingInterface. The interface then sends message 1.1, a receiving request, to the InventoryRouter. This router represents the point where the incoming operation is directed through the backend's role-controlled route. Its nested messages identify authorization as a necessary check before the receiveStock operation is passed to InventoryService.The service processes the receiving request and sends the save-and-commit interaction to Sequelize/MySQL, where the receipt and balance records are stored. The database returns the receipt result, which is propagated back through the service and interface so the staff member receives a response. Unlike Figure 12, which arranges messages along lifelines over time, this diagram emphasizes the participating objects and the links between them. Its numbering still preserves the causal order from staff submission to authorization, stock processing, persistence, and the final receipt response.

Interaction Overview Diagram/Figure 15. Overview of Inventory Receiving InteractionsFigure 15 combines an activity-level workflow with references to smaller interactions involved in receiving inventory. The process begins when a user opens the inventory workspace and enters the Authenticate and Authorize interaction. Within this referenced interaction, Inventory Staff send identity or role information to Access Checks, which consults the user records needed to process the request. The following decision determines whether the user can proceed. If access is denied, the system displays an access-denied message and the current attempt ends.An authorized user proceeds to the Receive Inventory Stock interaction, which is expanded in the sequence shown in Figure 12. In this stage, the Receiving UI submits delivery information to Stock Service, which coordinates the required processing with the models and MySQL database. Once receiving succeeds, the final interaction retrieves inventory data and refreshes the displayed balances. The overview intentionally omits the fine details of validation, duplicate-request checks, and transaction handling; those details belong to the referenced receiving interaction. Its purpose is to show how authorization, receiving, and screen refresh fit into one larger workflow.

Timing Diagram/Figure 16. Timing of the Stock Receiving ProcessFigure 16 provides an illustrative timing view of a stock-receiving operation across Inventory Staff, the Receiving UI, Access Checks, Stock Service, and Sequelize/MySQL. The stepped lines indicate when each participant is active during the example interaction. The staff member first submits a delivery, after which the interface sends the request and the access component performs authorization. Stock Service then carries out the validation and receiving work, while the persistence layer participates in locking and writing or committing the related records. Near the end, the interface displays the result for the user.The horizontal axis spans zero to four seconds, but these values are provided only to make the order and overlap of activity visible. They are not benchmark measurements, promised response times, or performance requirements. The main point of the timing view is the coordination between stages: authorization occurs before protected stock processing, database activity supports the stock operation, and the result is displayed after processing completes.

Requirement Diagram (SysML)/Figure 17. Requirements of the Inventory ModuleFigure 17 presents a SysML requirement view that traces the overall purpose of the inventory module to five more specific expectations. The top-level requirement, INV-00 Inventory Management, states that the system should support accurate and controlled stock operations. The deriveReqt relationships show how this broad objective is broken down into requirements that can be associated with implementation responsibilities. INV-01, Access Control, limits stock-changing operations to approved Inventory or Admin users and is satisfied by Access Middleware. INV-02, Reliable Receiving, requires related receiving records to be committed together and repeated requests not to duplicate stock; Stock Receiving Service is identified as the responsible component.

The remaining requirements address operational integrity after stock enters the system. INV-03, Safe Availability, protects reserved inventory and excludes expired or held batches from usable stock; the diagram links this requirement to Stock/Availability Services. INV-04, Controlled Counts, requires stale counts to be rejected and approval policy to be followed, with Count/Review Services providing the related behavior. INV-05, Traceable History, requires quantity changes, responsible actors, and reasons to be recorded, and is linked to Movement Records. The satisfy relationships make each requirement traceable to a named implementation element. The figure is a design-level statement of intended responsibilities; it does not by itself constitute test evidence that every requirement has been verified.
